newsitem.title: CHINA: China moves to scrap "counter-revolutionary" tag.
newsitem.headline: China moves to scrap "counter-revolutionary" tag.

text.p: China on Thursday edged away from its radical communist past by unveiling a major revision of its criminal law that would scrap "counter-revolutionary" crimes.

Officials said changes set for approval by the National People's Congress, or parliament, would drag the 17-year-old criminal code into the 1990s by listing offences such as money laundering, computer crime and insider trading.

Crimes previously considered counter-revolutionary would either be reclassified as offences endangering state security or as ordinary crimes, said Wang Hanbin, vice-chairman of the congress' Standing Committee.

"Revision of the crimes of counter-revolution is made out of the consideration that China has left the revolutionary era to enter the era of socialist construction and modernisation," Wang said in a speech to the annual session of the congress.

While crimes involving collusion with foreign countries would not be changed under the revised law, anti-state offences aimed at subverting the government or overthrowing the socialist system would be clarified and made more specific, he said.

"This will definitely serve to deal more telling blows at criminal activities designed to jeopardise state security," he told nearly 3,000 delegates in Beijing's Stalinist-era Great Hall of the People.
Beijing has long used the crime of counter-revolution as a catch-all to punish anyone whose opinions are judged hostile to the state or ruling Communist Party.
Some analysts said the newly clarified offences were likely to be used in the same way.
The scrapping of a crime clearly linked to China's revolutionary past had long been pushed by reformers anxious to modernise the nation's fledgling penal code.

Moves to scrap the offence were stalled by the political chill that followed the crushing of student-led pro-democracy protests in Beijing in 1989 -- when many demonstrators were convicted of counter-revolutionary crimes.
Wang said other changes to the criminal law, which the largely rubber-stamp parliament is scheduled to approve next week, would seek to curb the rise of new kinds of wrongdoing.
Offences such as creating computer viruses, breaking into information networks, insider trading on China's new financial markets and money-laundering would all be addressed, he said.
The amendments took aim at criminal groups that were "running amok in the neighbourhoods, perpetrating outrages, riding roughshod over and slaughtering people", he said.

The revisions were also intended to aid Beijing's fight against pro-independence sentiment in its restive far-western regions, with jail terms of up to 10 years prescribed for anyone who incites ethnic hatred or tries to undermine unity.
Some of the new offences of endangering state security would also help crack down on separatists, Wang said.

"These regulations focus on the great danger currently facing state security from subversive activities such as joint foreign and domestic action to promote 'Westernisation' and 'splittism'," he said.

Human rights activists have long condemned China's frequent use of the death penalty, but while Wang said the revisions barred the execution of offenders under the age of 18, he dismissed calls for more limited use of capital punishment.
"The fact that the situation in public order is far from stable and economic offences become more and more serious shows the conditions for such a reduction do not exist yet," he said.
